title: The Stoics
summary: Stoicism is a philosophical school that arose in Athens around 300 BC and flourished in Rome. Its central idea: we do not control events, but we can govern how we understand them and how we respond to them. The aim is to live “in accordance with nature” — that is, with reason, with integrity, and in connection with other people.
onEmotions: The Stoics distinguished “first movements” — involuntary bodily responses like trembling or tears, which are not in our power and for which no one is to blame — from “passions,” states in which we have already assented to a mistaken judgment such as “something terrible has happened.” The ideal was not numbness but apatheia — freedom from overwhelming passions — together with the eupatheiai, the good feelings: calm joy, reasonable caution, goodwill. For a Stoic, working with a feeling means carefully examining your own “impression”: what do I actually think about what is happening, and is it true?

anxiety.text: “When I see a man anxious, I ask: what does he want?” Epictetus told his students. If he did not want something outside his power, how could he be anxious? This is no reproach: an anxious mind is simply trying to shield you ahead of time from a future that does not exist yet. Epictetus considered one distinction the most important of all: our judgments, intentions and actions are up to us; other people's decisions, health, and the outcome of events are not. Anxiety often grows when we try to hold the second kind of thing in our hands. A Stoic doesn't ask you to stop feeling; he suggests gently sorting the worry: this part is mine, and I can do something about it today; this part is not mine, and I can let it go without ceasing to care about it. Then anxiety becomes not a verdict but a signal pointing to where your next step lies.
anxiety.practice: Fold a finger for each part of the worry and ask, as Epictetus did: “Mine or not mine?” For what is yours, name one step for today; let what is not yours go on an exhale as you open your hand.

quote.text: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the opinions about things.
quote.author: Epictetus

fear.text: “Is this what I was afraid of?” Seneca would ask himself, deliberately spending a few days on the scantiest food and in rough clothing. He wrote to Lucilius that many things frighten us more than they can hurt us — and your fear, too, is probably painting the disaster in more detail than it has. Still, fear is an ancient protector: it switches on to guard what you hold dear. The Stoics proposed an exercise later called “premeditatio malorum” — thinking through misfortunes in advance: calmly picture a difficult outcome and ask yourself what you would do and what strengths you could lean on. Paradoxically, looking straight at what frightens us often weakens its hold: a vague threat turns into a concrete difficulty that one can live with. Stoicism doesn't promise that there will be nothing left to fear. It reminds you that your capacity to meet whatever happens with dignity stays with you, whatever the outcome.
fear.practice: Do a short premeditatio: close your eyes and imagine that the frightening thing has happened. Live one minute of that day in your mind — what are you doing, who is near, what do you still have? Then open your eyes and notice where you actually are.

quote.text: There are more things likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
quote.author: Seneca

sadness.text: In army camps on the Danube, Marcus Aurelius kept his notes, and there is a good deal of quiet sorrow in them — about mortality, about teachers who had died, about people. The sadness that comes when something dear turns out differently than we hoped was familiar to him too. The Stoics are sometimes imagined as people who forbade themselves to be sad, but that isn't quite right. Seneca acknowledged that the soul has “first movements” — an involuntary heaviness, tears — that are not in our power and need not be a source of shame. The Stoic work begins later: noticing what thought the sadness carries with it. Sometimes behind it is a simple “I'm sorry this happened,” and sometimes “everything will always be bad.” The first can simply be lived through; the second is worth checking, because it is already a judgment, and judgments are in our power. Marcus Aurelius often reminded himself that everything in the world flows and changes. This thought can be a comfort: your present state is also part of the flow, and it is not forever.
sadness.practice: Take a few slow breaths out, and with each one say silently: “This too is part of the flow.” Then ask what thought comes with your sadness, and note: is it a fact or a prediction?

grief.text: When Marcia's son died, Seneca wrote her a long letter — three years later, because her grief still had not let go. Grief is love that has nowhere left to go, and the Stoics understood this. Seneca, who himself suffered many losses, wrote letters of consolation to his friends and did not demand stony calm from them. He allowed for tears, but advised not letting grief swallow the whole of life — and, above all, keeping in memory what had been given. The Stoics reminded us that everything dear to us is given not as our property but for a time — as if on loan from nature. The thought sounds stern, but it holds a comfort too: the time you spent together was real, and no one can take it away now. Grief is the consequence of attachment, and the Stoics valued attachment too. Gradually, the pain can turn into grateful remembrance.
grief.practice: Tell someone — a friend, or simply the quiet room, out loud — one story about the person you lost that you love. This is what Seneca urged Marcia to do: not to fall silent about him, but to remember.

quote.text: Let not the eyes be dry when we have lost a friend, nor let them overflow.
quote.author: Seneca

loneliness.text: Marcus Aurelius compared a person who cuts himself off from others to a severed hand lying apart from the body — and added at once that a person, unlike a hand, can grow back (VIII, 34). That is why loneliness hurts so much: we are social by nature. The Stoics taught oikeiosis, “appropriation” or “making one's own”: from birth we reach toward caring for ourselves, and then this circle widens to include those close to us, our fellow citizens and, ideally, all of humanity. Marcus Aurelius wrote that we are made for working together, like feet, hands or eyelids. Your longing for closeness is the voice of human nature itself. At the same time, the Stoics valued being able to keep good company with oneself: Seneca advised spending time with the thoughts of worthy people, reading them as if in conversation. Loneliness can be taken as a reminder: I am part of a larger whole even when no one is nearby, and every kind thing I do is a thread tying me to others.
loneliness.practice: Do one small thing for someone today: hold a door, send a short “how are you?”, thank a cashier by name. That is what “growing back” looks like — one thread at a time.

anger.text: Seneca tells of Plato: angry with a slave, he froze with his hand raised and explained to a friend that he was punishing an angry man — himself (On Anger, III, 12). Anger flares when something important is touched — fairness, boundaries, dignity — and the Stoics did not treat it as a trifle. Seneca devoted an entire treatise, On Anger, to this feeling and took the subject very seriously. He distinguished the first jolt — the rush of heat, the urge to respond, which arises on its own and for which you are not responsible — from what follows, when the mind assents to the thought “I have been wronged, and this must be repaid.” Seneca considered delay the best remedy for anger: anger weakens if you wait. Marcus Aurelius began his mornings by reminding himself that he would meet difficult people that day, that they act this way out of ignorance, and that he is nonetheless bound to them by a shared nature. The Stoics would say you can accept anger as a signal about what you value — without rushing to hand it the wheel.
anger.practice: When you feel anger surging, do what Plato did in Seneca's story: freeze. Lower your hands, take three slow breaths out, and only then decide whether and how to respond.

quote.text: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial.
quote.author: Marcus Aurelius

shame.text: Crates, the teacher of the Stoa's founder, made young Zeno carry a pot of lentil soup down a crowded street — and then smashed it with his staff. Dripping, Zeno ran off, and Crates called after him: “Why run away? Nothing terrible has happened to you!” Shame is something we want to hide, even though everyone feels it. The Stoics help us look at it from another side. For Epictetus, a person's worth is determined not by the opinion of others, not by appearance, and not by success, but by how they use their prohairesis — the capacity to choose and to judge. Everything else the Stoics called “indifferent”: not trivial, but something that makes you neither a good nor a bad person. If your shame is tied to someone else's gaze, a Stoic would ask: is another person's opinion within my power? If shame points to something you did and regret, it is a sign that being decent matters to you — which means your capacity for good is intact. Epictetus reminded us that nothing great comes into being all at once: we learn all our lives.
shame.practice: Recall a time you felt ashamed a couple of years ago. Ask yourself, as Crates would: “What terrible thing actually happened to me?” Notice what is left of that shame today.

guilt.text: Every evening, when the lamp was out and his wife, knowing his habit, had fallen silent, Seneca held a court on himself — reviewing the day he had lived (On Anger, III, 36). Guilt says the same thing that court does: you care how your actions affect others. The Stoics regarded almost everyone as a prokopton, “one who is making progress” — a student on the way to wisdom, for whom mistakes are inevitable. Seneca held this evening court without cruelty — to understand, not to punish — and ended with words like “see that you do not do that again; this time I pardon you.” The past, according to the Stoics, is no longer in our power; what is in our power is what we do now: apologize, make amends, act differently next time. Guilt turned into such action has done its job. Guilt that gnaws endlessly no longer helps you or the people you hurt.
guilt.practice: Tonight before sleep, hold Seneca's court — short and merciful: one misstep, one lesson, one sentence of forgiveness. Say them to yourself once the light is off.

envy.text: “What does lettuce cost?” Epictetus asks. An obol, say: whoever paid the obol got the lettuce, and you, not paying, kept your obol (Enchiridion, 25). When someone else's success stings, it hurts, and it doesn't make you any worse a person. Everything has its price, he said: if someone was invited to a banquet and you weren't, it means he paid for the invitation — with flattery, time, effort. If you didn't pay that price, it's odd to demand the goods; but you still have what you kept. Moreover, for a Stoic the true good is virtue: wisdom, justice, courage, moderation — while wealth, fame and recognition are merely “preferred indifferents.” They are pleasant to have, but whether you live well does not depend on them. You can take envy as a hint about what you truly want — and ask what price you yourself are willing to pay for it.
envy.practice: Picture what you envy on a market stall with a price tag: how many hours, concessions and efforts did it cost the other person? Decide whether you want to buy at that price — or keep your obol.

emptiness.text: “How long the same things? I will wake, sleep, eat, be cold, be warm” — this is how Seneca records the complaint of people for whom life has come to feel empty (Letter XXIV). It is a heavy state, when strength has gone and meaning seems lost, and you don't need to blame yourself for it. The Stoics didn't describe apathy in the modern sense: their word apatheia meant something else — freedom from overwhelming passions. But even in emptiness, the Stoics held, a person keeps a small foothold: the ability to choose how to relate to this moment. Marcus Aurelius admitted to himself that it was hard to get up in the morning, and reminded himself: I am rising to do the work of a human being. Not some great work — just the next one. The Stoics believed that everyone is connected to the common whole, the logos, the rational order of the world, and that even a small act of kindness or care brings us back into that connection. You don't have to find meaning all at once; you can make it little by little.
emptiness.practice: Get up and do one piece of “a human being's work,” as Marcus Aurelius called it: pour some water, open a window, make the bed. Note to yourself: “I chose this.”

confusion.text: The Greek word enchiridion means “that which is kept at hand” — it could name a dagger or a handbook, something you grab in a difficult moment. When the familiar map of your life no longer matches the terrain, such a thing at hand is especially needed. It is an honest state: you can see that the old answers don't fit. Epictetus began his Handbook with a single distinction: some things are in our power, others are not. When everything is mixed up, this distinction works like a compass. You don't need to understand the whole picture at once: it is enough to find what depends on you right now. Epictetus also spoke of “roles”: each of us is someone's son or daughter, friend, worker, citizen, and each role suggests what is fitting to do. Confusion can be accepted as a pause before a more precise choice. Better decisions are often born from it than from hasty certainty.
confusion.practice: Name three of your roles out loud — for example, “friend,” “daughter,” “neighbor.” For each, ask as Epictetus would: what is fitting to do in this role today? Pick the simplest.

fatigue.text: Seneca recalls that Socrates was not ashamed to play with children, nor Scipio to dance, and writes: the mind must be given rest, and it will rise from it better and keener (On Tranquility of Mind, 17). If you are worn out, it is a sign that you have been carrying a lot for a long time. The Stoics are often pictured as people of unbending will, but Seneca wrote that the mind needs rest like a field: without a break it becomes exhausted. He praised walks, a change of activity, friendly conversation, and even an unhurried meal shared with friends. Epictetus, in turn, helps us see where part of our tiredness may come from: we spend our strength on what is not in our power — on controlling other people's opinions, results, the future. Letting go of this is not giving up; it means no longer hauling a load that was never yours to begin with. The Stoics would say that conserving your strength is also part of living “in accordance with nature”: you are not a machine but a living being with limits, and respecting them is an expression of reason.
fatigue.practice: Let your mind lie fallow: for five minutes do nothing — sit, rest your hands on your knees, look out the window. If a thought about tasks comes, tell it: “Later.”

boredom.text: Seneca describes people who travel to the coast and at once long to be back in the city — “thus each person flees from himself” (On Tranquility of Mind, 2). Boredom can be agonizing: time drags and nothing brings joy. You need to change your soul, not the sky above you, he replied to a friend who complained that his journeys did not help. For a Stoic, boredom may suggest that your attention has drifted into waiting for something external to entertain you. The Stoics proposed bringing attention back to the present: Marcus Aurelius advised doing each task wholly, fully present, without being distracted by busyness. You can take boredom as an invitation: notice what is happening right now, and ask what this time might serve.
boredom.practice: Wash one cup the way Marcus Aurelius advised doing every act — as if it were the last of your life: the warm water, the weight of the cup, the sound. One cup, wholly.

joy.text: “Above all, Lucilius, learn how to feel joy,” Seneca writes in his twenty-third letter. Your joy right now is exactly what the Stoics trained for, not something they forbade. On the contrary, among the eupatheiai, the good feelings of the sage, joy was named first — chara in Greek, gaudium in Latin. In the same letter he notes that true joy is a serious matter: it grows from within, from a good life, rather than depending on fortune's chance gifts. The Stoics distinguished this deep joy from fleeting pleasure, which disappears along with its external cause. That doesn't mean you can't be glad of external things: you can, just without clutching them in a death grip. A Stoic would say that your joy is especially steady when it is connected with what you did, what you understood, how you treated others — with what no one can take away.
joy.practice: Share with one person what made you glad today — and add what part you yourself played in it.

quote.text: Above all, my dear Lucilius, make this your business: learn how to feel joy.
quote.author: Seneca

love.text: Seneca wrote to Lucilius that he makes a friend not so as to have someone to sit by his bedside, but so as to have someone at whose bedside he can sit (Letter IX). The tenderness you feel is something the Stoics, despite their stern image, valued highly. They considered attachment to family and friends natural: it is the same oikeiosis, care that widens from oneself to those close to us. Epictetus did, admittedly, give a difficult piece of advice: when you embrace someone you love, remember that they are mortal and not given to you forever. It sounds cold, but the point is different — such remembrance makes tenderness more alive and attentive, guarding against the habit of taking loved ones for granted. Seneca called friendship a great good. The Stoics would say that love is purest when it holds more wishing well for the other than wishing to possess.
love.practice: Tell one person close to you one specific thing you value in them — out loud or in a short message. Epictetus would remind you: this day together is a gift, not a given.

gratitude.text: “From my grandfather Verus: kindness and an even temper” — so begins a book that a Roman emperor wrote only for himself (I, 1). The Stoics cultivated gratitude deliberately, as a skill. The first book of Marcus Aurelius's Meditations consists entirely of thanks: to his grandfather, his mother, his teachers, his friends — to each for a specific quality or lesson he received from them. The emperor who ruled a vast realm began his private notes not with his worries but with a list of what others had given him. Seneca wrote a treatise, On Benefits, and considered ingratitude one of the most widespread vices, while the ability to receive good and remember it was a sign of a healthy soul. For a Stoic, gratitude restores our sense of connection with the whole: we did not make ourselves. It also helps with acceptance: even on a hard day you can find what was given, and it balances what was taken away.
gratitude.practice: Like Marcus Aurelius, write one line in the form “From … — …”: from whom, and what quality or lesson you received.

hope.text: “You will cease to fear if you cease to hope” — Seneca quotes these words of the philosopher Hecato in his fifth letter to Lucilius, and they sound almost cruel. Hope helps us hold on, and in hard times it is especially precious, so it's worth looking honestly at these words. Hope and fear, Seneca writes, walk together like a prisoner and his guard, bound by one chain. He meant that they are two sides of one state: a mind suspended over a future that does not depend on us. This is not a call to despair — quite the opposite. The Stoics proposed moving our footing from the future into the present: not “everything will surely be fine,” but “whatever happens, I will try to meet it with dignity.” Such hope in yourself, in your ability to respond, is sturdier than hope in circumstances. You can go on hoping for good things — just without making your inner steadiness wholly dependent on the outcome.
hope.practice: Say your hope out loud the Stoic way, with a “reserve clause”: “I hope that… — and if not, I can…” Listen to how the second half sounds.

quote.text: You will cease to fear if you cease to hope.
quote.author: Seneca (quoting Hecato)

nostalgia.text: Seneca divided life into three times — what was, what is, and what will be — and observed that only over the first has fortune lost all power. In the sweet, slightly sad longing for the past there is a lot of love for what you have lived. In On the Shortness of Life he calls the past the most secure part of our life: it cannot be taken away. What was good will forever remain as having been. At the same time, Marcus Aurelius constantly reminded himself that we can live only in the present — the only time we truly have. A Stoic would say that nostalgia can be accepted as a grateful remembrance that nourishes, rather than an attempt to bring back what cannot return. The past becomes not a place you want to escape to, but a store from which you draw strength and an understanding of what you hold dear.
nostalgia.practice: Hold something from that time in your hands — a photo, a letter, an old cup — for a minute. Ask: what was valuable in it, and where does that value have a place now?

craving.text: Zeno, the founder of the Stoa, showed the path from impression to action on his own hand: an open palm is an impression, slightly bent fingers are assent, a clenched fist is firm conviction. A craving — that sharp “I want it right now” — is like a hand that clenches by itself, and there is nothing shameful in its strength. The Stoics described in detail a mechanism very much like it. First comes an “impression” — a picture of relief, of taste, of calm. Then the mind either gives it “assent” (synkatathesis in Greek) or does not. Epictetus advised not assenting right away, but saying to the impression something like: “Wait, let me look at what you are.” Between impulse and action there is a gap, and your freedom lives in it. The craving itself may not disappear — the Stoics didn't demand that you not feel it; they suggested not confusing a sensation with a command. Every wave you have waited out is practice, not an exam, and its outcome does not determine your worth.
craving.practice: When the craving rolls in, open your palm like Zeno and keep it open while you take ten slow breaths. Say to yourself: “This is an impression. I haven't given my assent.”

addiction.text: Epictetus advised his students to count the days: “I used to be angry every day, then every other day, then every third, then every fourth” (Discourses, II, 18). Addiction is not a moral failure but a loop that took a long time to form and holds on tight. The Stoics thought a great deal about habit. Epictetus observed that every capacity is strengthened by the corresponding actions: walking by walking, running by running. So the loop of addiction is something that has been trained many times over, not your “nature” — and in the same way, step by step, something else can be trained. Epictetus, himself a former slave, considered freedom the chief business of philosophy: free is the one whose “ruling part,” the hegemonikon, has not been handed over to the power of things. At the same time, the Stoics spoke with respect of the prokoptontes, “those making progress” — people on the way rather than at the goal. In this picture, setbacks do not cancel the path. Even Seneca wrote his letters to Lucilius as a fellow traveler, not as a mentor who had already overcome everything.
addiction.practice: Count as Epictetus did — not in years but in days and hours: name out loud one recent hour when the loop loosened. If you'd like, tell someone who understands about it — a friend, or a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: “Do not be ashamed of being helped,” Marcus Aurelius wrote to himself: a lame soldier cannot climb the wall alone in an assault, but with a comrade he can (VII, 7). The morning after can be doubly hard — the body aches, your head swirls with anxiety, shame, fragments of last night — and such a morning deserves not a verdict but gentleness. The Stoics distinguished “first movements” — the body's involuntary response: trembling, heaviness, turmoil — from the judgments we add on top: “I'm awful,” “everything is ruined.” The first simply needs to be waited out while you take care of yourself. The second can be examined. Marcus Aurelius advised separating the bare event from the evaluation: “this is what happened” — without writing a verdict onto it. Seneca told how every evening he reviewed the day that had passed, asking himself without self-flagellation: what did I do wrong, what can be put right? Yesterday is no longer in your power; your response to it today is.
hangover.practice: Sit down, put your feet on the floor and breathe slowly. With each exhale, separate fact from verdict as the Stoics did: keep “this is what happened yesterday” and let go of “so I'm awful.”

euphoria.text: “Receive without arrogance, let go without struggle,” Marcus Aurelius wrote to himself — a man to whom fortune had given more than to almost anyone (VIII, 33). Your burst is vivid, there can be much that is real in it — a taste for life, a sense of strength — and there's no need to spoil it with suspicion. The Stoics distinguished the “passion” of pleasure — an excitement resting on the thought “this is the most important thing, I need more of it” — from the eupatheia of joy, which is calm and rests on what is within us. A Stoic doesn't extinguish the high but asks it a small question: what are you resting on? If on something external — luck, praise, an event — then, like everything external, the high will come and go. Marcus Aurelius constantly reminded himself that everything flows and changes. Here that thought doesn't cool things down but sets you free: you can enjoy without clutching and without promising yourself it will always be like this. Then the way down will be gentler too.
euphoria.practice: In the middle of the high, take three slow breaths and say Marcus's words to yourself: “Receive without arrogance, let go without struggle.” Then name out loud exactly what you are glad about.

crash.text: Time is a river of events, Marcus Aurelius wrote: no sooner has something appeared than it is swept away, and another is carried along (IV, 43). The drop after a celebration, a success or a vivid evening can be unexpectedly steep, and it is not your fault: this is often how waves work. The Stoics would say the comedown is especially painful because of an involuntary comparison: “yesterday was like that, and today is like this — so something must be broken.” But both yesterday's high and today's low belong to the “external” — to what comes and goes. Marcus Aurelius looked at life as a stream of changes and saw in it not a threat but the natural order of things. The Stoic foothold is not mood, but what you can do and how you relate to what is happening. Even on a gray day, small things remain within reach: doing one task honestly, being kind to someone — yourself included. The low is part of the flow too, and it will pass as well.
crash.practice: Do one honest small thing — make the bed, answer one message, take out the trash — and note: “This depended on me, and I did it.”

panic.text: Aulus Gellius describes a storm at sea: a Stoic philosopher on board turned pale, and afterward showed his fellow passengers a passage from Epictetus — even the sage flinches at the sudden, but does not assent to the thought “I am lost.” A wave of panic is truly frightening: your heart pounds, you can't get enough air — and it is not your fault that this is happening. The Stoics knew that the body can respond before reason does — they called these “first movements”: trembling, pallor, ragged breathing come without our consent, and not even the sage is immune to them. There is comfort in this: the wave itself is not your failure. The Stoic part of the work is gently not adding a second layer of judgments like “this will never end.” A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. You can meet it like bad weather: not arguing with it, but anchoring yourself in the present moment — the only one, as Marcus Aurelius wrote, that we actually have.
panic.practice: Take hold of something solid — the edge of a table, the back of a chair — and feel its firmness. Make each exhale longer than the inhale and repeat silently, like the Stoic on the ship: “The body is shaking. I am here.” Name five objects you can see.

dread.text: Marcus Aurelius would run through the departed in his mind — physicians who frowned over the sick, astrologers who foretold other people's deaths, Alexander the Great — and calmly add: they too (IV, 48). The thought of our finitude and the question “what's the point of all this” can come over you suddenly, and they speak of the depth of your mind. The Stoics did not turn away from these questions. Marcus Aurelius often thought about the fleetingness of everything — and drew from it not the conclusion that nothing matters, but that the present is precious: since time is limited, each day can be lived attentively and kindly. For the Stoics, meaning lies not somewhere outside, in a guarantee of eternity, but in the very way of living — with reason, justly, in connection with others. Marcus wrote that people are made for working together, like hands, feet or eyelids. The abyss doesn't vanish because of this, but beside it a foothold appears: this day, this person, this good deed. That is enough to keep going.
dread.practice: Step outside for a minute or go to a window and look at the sky. Then lower your gaze to something close — a tree, a passerby, your own hand — and tell yourself: “This day. This task.”

fomo.text: Epictetus suggested behaving in life as at a banquet where the dishes are passed around. When other people's lives are visible around the clock in your feed, it's easy to feel that everyone is at the best tables and you are not. A dish reaches you — take a moderate portion; it passes by — don't hold it back; it hasn't reached you yet — don't stretch for it from afar, wait. Epictetus also reminded us that everything has its price: someone was invited to the party because they paid for the invitation with time, flattery, effort — and you kept something of your own. And you are “where you should be,” at least in one sense: only here do you have access to what depends on you. Someone else's feast doesn't cancel your own table.
fomo.practice: When “I'm missing out” stings, put your phone face down and look around like a guest at Epictetus's banquet: what dish is in front of me right now? Give it five minutes of real attention.

sleepless.text: Seneca once lodged right above a public bathhouse: the grunts of athletes, the slap of the masseur, the cries of the pastry seller — and he wrote that the noise did not bother him as long as it was quiet within (Letter LVI). At three in the morning, thoughts have a way of becoming louder and darker than by day, noisier than any bathhouse. The Stoics would suggest not settling big questions at night: judgments born in darkness and fatigue are worth postponing until morning and examining in daylight. Seneca wrote that every evening he reviewed the day that had passed and then let it go — and that sleep after such a review is more peaceful. You don't have to argue with every nighttime thought. You can politely tell it, “I'll hear you out tomorrow,” and return to your breathing. In the morning many of these thoughts will turn out smaller than they seemed.
sleepless.practice: Whisper to the persistent thought: “I'll hear you out in the morning.” Rest a palm on your belly and count your exhales to ten, then start again from one.

betrayal.text: The finest general of Marcus Aurelius, Avidius Cassius, raised a rebellion against him; when it was over, according to Cassius Dio, the emperor burned the conspirators' letters unread. The blow came from where there was trust — that is why betrayal wounds so deeply, and the Stoics don't suggest pretending nothing happened. In the Meditations Marcus reminds himself again and again that people act badly because they are mistaken about good and evil — and that this is their error, not a measure of your worth. Another person's act cannot make you worse: how you respond remains in your power. At the same time, a Stoic is not obliged to trust again someone who betrayed them — reasonable caution is also one of the eupatheiai, the good feelings. You can grieve the lost trust, protect yourself, and not let bitterness take over everything, all at the same time.
betrayal.practice: Tell one person you trust about what happened — not to decide what to do, but to separate out loud: what they did, and what remains mine no matter what.

jealousy.text: Epictetus advised never saying of someone close “I have lost them,” only “I have given them back”: those we love are given to us not as property but for a time (Enchiridion, 11). Jealousy is a mixture of fear of loss, pain and insecurity, and behind it lies an attachment that is precious to you. The Stoics would say jealousy is agonizing also because it is aimed at what by its very nature is not in our power: another person's feelings and choices. Epictetus's advice sounds stern, but there is relief in it too: you don't need to — and can't — control another person. What is in your power is something else: being honest, speaking about your feelings, caring for the relationship and for yourself. Stoic love is not possession but attentive presence beside a free human being.
jealousy.practice: Open both hands: in the right, place in your mind what you know for certain; in the left, what your imagination is filling in. Lower the left. What one honest conversation remains in the right?

resentment.text: Cato was once struck in the baths by someone who didn't recognize him; when the man came to apologize, Cato replied, “I don't remember being struck” (Seneca, On Anger, II, 32). An old grudge is heavy, and behind it there is usually a real injustice — forgetting it the way Cato did is rarely possible. The Stoics would take it seriously — and would also ask: whom is it hurting more right now? In On Anger, Seneca shows how resentment grows when we retell ourselves the insult again and again, adding ever new interpretations to the fact. Marcus Aurelius wrote that the best way to defend yourself against someone who wronged you is not to become like them. Letting go of resentment doesn't mean saying “everything was fine,” or necessarily making peace. It means taking back the part of your attention that for years has gone into an old wound. Your judgment of what they did may stay the same — all that leaves is the endless rumination that torments you most of all.
resentment.practice: Try on Cato's phrase — “I don't remember being struck” — not as a lie but as an experiment: what would it be like not to carry this grudge for one minute? Notice what changes in your shoulders and breathing.

heartbreak.text: “Loss is nothing other than change,” Marcus Aurelius wrote (IX, 35), and the phrase is cold only at first glance. A breakup turns life upside down: habits, plans, the voice beside you all disappear — and a broken heart truly hurts. The Stoics recognized such “first movements” as natural. Consoling his friends, Seneca advised not forbidding yourself to grieve, but also not making grief the only content of your life. The Stoic view suggests holding two things together. The first: what was between you was real — Seneca wrote that the past is safe, and no one can take it away now. The second: the other person is free, and their choice is not a verdict on you. Your worth isn't decided by whether this love stayed with you. Gradually you can take back what is yours — friendships, work, caring for yourself — without hurrying the pain.
heartbreak.practice: Walk a familiar route for ten minutes and notice what has changed since last time: a sign, a tree, the light. Change around you — and in you — happens on its own; it doesn't need hurrying.

impostor.text: Seneca, the most widely read philosopher in Rome, called himself not a doctor but a patient lying in the same ward and sharing remedies with his neighbor (Letter XXVII). If you fear that you're about to be “found out,” this happens to very capable people too, and your very demandingness toward yourself speaks of conscientiousness. The Stoics would shift the question. Epictetus placed other people's opinions, reputation and recognition among the things “not in our power.” What is in our power is how we do our work: honestly, attentively. Epictetus even advised: if you want to make progress, be content to seem ignorant in external matters. The Stoics did not pretend to be sages — they called themselves “those making progress” and saw nothing shameful in it. You don't have to know everything already. Being a student of your craft is not a deception but an honest position, and there is no need to hide it.
impostor.practice: Tell a colleague or friend about one thing you are learning right now — just like that: “I'm still making progress at this.” Notice that the sky hasn't fallen.

self_hatred.text: “You” — this is how Marcus Aurelius addresses himself in the pages of the Meditations, and that voice is demanding but almost never cruel. If your inner critic sounds merciless, that is very hard, and you deserve support, not yet another verdict. The Stoics are sometimes imagined as stern judges of themselves, but their self-examination was different. Seneca described his evening review of the day as a conversation in which he said to himself: “see that you don't do that again; this time I pardon you.” He examined actions; he did not pass sentence on his whole person. In the Meditations, Marcus Aurelius also talks to himself — demandingly, but as to a friend: if something didn't work out, don't despair; come back to it again. For the Stoics, the voice insisting “I'm worthless” is not reason but a passion — that is, a mistaken judgment — and you are not at all obliged to agree with it.
self_hatred.practice: Say one of your inner critic's phrases out loud, then retell it the way Marcus Aurelius spoke to himself: “You got this part wrong. Come back and try again.”

helplessness.text: Legend has it that Epictetus's master was twisting his leg, and the slave said calmly, “You will break it”; when the leg broke, he added, “Didn't I tell you?” When it seems nothing can be changed, it is one of the most tormenting feelings there is. The Stoics didn't deny that a huge part of life is not in our power — on the contrary, that is exactly where they began. But their distinction works in both directions. Even when circumstances don't depend on you, a thin but real area remains: how you understand what is happening, where you direct your attention, how you treat yourself and others. Epictetus, a former slave who was also lame, knew powerlessness firsthand — and perhaps that is exactly why he so valued this small island of freedom. Helplessness before the large does not cancel strength in the small. Sometimes the only thing you can do is live today gently. That is already a lot.
helplessness.practice: Think of Epictetus and find your own “small island”: name three things that are still yours at this minute — your breath, your gaze, your next word. Choose one and do it with care.

quote.text: Some things are under our control, while others are not under our control.
quote.author: Epictetus

procrastination.text: “Claim yourself for yourself” — so begins Seneca's first letter to Lucilius: time is taken from us, stolen, and still more we lose ourselves by putting things off. Seneca didn't say this to shame anyone: behind “I can't get started” there is more often fear, fatigue or a task that is too big than laziness. Marcus Aurelius, judging by his notes, also found it hard to get up in the morning and coaxed himself: I am rising to do the work of a human being. The Stoic solution is to focus not on the whole task but on the next action: do what is in front of you as if it were the only thing. To begin means to take a very small first step, not to conquer everything at once.
procrastination.practice: Set a timer for five minutes and do only the first bit of the task, telling yourself, as Marcus Aurelius did at dawn: “I am rising to do the work of a human being.” When the timer rings, you may stop.

quote.text: Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time.
quote.author: Seneca

uprooted.text: Seneca spent eight years in exile on Corsica, a bare, rocky island, and from there wrote a consolation to his own mother. Losing your home means losing not only an address but the language of the streets, familiar faces, the ground beneath your feet — it is real grief. The Stoics knew it from the inside: Musonius Rufus and Epictetus were also banished from Rome. In that consolation Seneca said that wherever we are cast, the nature we all share and our own soul remain with us. The Stoics called themselves “cosmopolitans” — citizens of the world: a person belongs not only to their own city but to the vast community of all human beings. This doesn't cancel homesickness, but it offers a second foothold: you haven't fallen out of the world, you are in another part of it, and here too there are people you can grow close to.
uprooted.practice: Walk around your new place and find one thing that is there wherever you are cast — the sky, a tree, fresh bread at a bakery. Seneca would say: this is the world we all share, and it is yours too.

overload.text: “Whoever is everywhere is nowhere,” Seneca warned Lucilius, who was devouring book after book (Letter II): better a few things, but thoroughly — so that what you read has time to become your own. When there are more news stories, messages and opinions than your head can hold, fatigue and irritation are natural. Epictetus advised testing every “impression” before letting it in: what are you, and do you concern me? And Marcus Aurelius observed that most of what we say and do is not necessary, and advised asking ourselves before each of them: is this needed? The Stoic filter is simple: most of the noise is not in your power and does not require your assent.
overload.practice: Before your next tap on the feed, hold your finger over the screen and ask, as Marcus Aurelius did: “Is this necessary?” If not, carry the phone into another room for ten minutes.

unreality.text: “This purple robe is sheep's wool dyed with shellfish blood” — this is how Marcus Aurelius trained himself to see things “as they are,” without glitter or fog (VI, 13). When everything around you — or you yourself — seems not quite real, as if behind glass, it's a strange and often unsettling experience, and it can be talked about calmly. The Stoics didn't describe it in modern terms, but they would probably say that the foothold in such moments lies not in understanding at once what is happening, but in what is always close at hand: the body, the present moment, the next task. Such sober naming can help restore contact: here is the table, here is the cup, here is my hand. The world hasn't gone anywhere, and you can return to it step by step.
unreality.practice: Pick up the nearest object and describe it under your breath, as Marcus Aurelius would: “This is a mug — fired clay, white, warm on one side.” Then do the same for the chair beneath you and the floor under your feet.

awe.text: “The view from above” is the name given to an exercise of Marcus Aurelius: rise in thought and look down on the earth — armies, fields, weddings, markets, births and deaths — all at once (VII, 48). Awe before a starry sky, the sea or music is something the Stoics valued highly. For them the world is a single living order, pervaded by logos, the rational principle, and the human being is part of it. This “view from above” makes small worries smaller and the connection with the whole more tangible. Seneca wrote that contemplating nature lifts up the soul and leads it out of the cramped quarters of everyday cares. For a Stoic, reverence is not an escape from life but a reminder of its scale: you are a small but real part of a vast whole. This feeling can simply be lived, without hurrying to explain it.
awe.practice: Close your eyes and do the “view from above”: rise above the room, the house, the city, until the earth becomes a globe. Stay there for a minute — then slowly return to your body.

relief.text: Epictetus said that difficulties show what a person is: like a wrestling trainer, God has matched you with a tough young opponent (Discourses, I, 24). Now that the bout is over and the tension has let go, the warm wave of relief is pleasant simply to live through. The Stoics would say relief often shows how much strength went into waiting for disaster: Seneca noted more than once that imagination torments us more than events themselves. Relief is a good moment to see this without reproach: “so that's how much I was carrying.” The Stoics also valued gratitude that things turned out all right — not as a duty, but as a natural continuation of relief. You might also notice that the difficulty you went through left you something: experience, knowledge of your own strength. And for now, you can simply breathe out and allow yourself to rest.
relief.practice: Take three long exhales, like a wrestler after a bout, letting your shoulders drop with each one. On the last, tell yourself: “That's behind me.”

calm.text: “People seek retreats in the country, by the sea, in the mountains,” Marcus Aurelius wrote, “yet at any hour you can withdraw into yourself” (IV, 3). The Stoics considered this quiet state one of the fruits of philosophy. They called it euthymia — good-heartedness, an even disposition of mind; Seneca devoted a whole treatise to it, On Tranquility of Mind. Stoic calm is not the absence of events but steadiness within, when you are not dependent on every wave outside. The calm you feel now is exactly an experience of such an inner refuge. It's worth remembering it with your body: how your breath, your shoulders, your gaze feel. Then on a hard day you'll have somewhere to return to.
calm.practice: For three minutes do nothing: sit as if in your “inner retreat” and simply notice your breath, your shoulders, your gaze. Remember this place — you can withdraw here on a hard day.

inspiration.text: “I feel, Lucilius, that I am not only being improved but transformed,” Seneca writes in his sixth letter, and in that phrase you can hear the surge of someone whose mind has caught fire. Inspiration is a lively surge when you want to act and create, and it is joyful in itself. The Stoics would say it reveals the rational nature of the human being, which strives toward action: Marcus Aurelius reminded himself that a person is born for work, not for lying snug under the blankets. Seneca constantly stressed that philosophy is tested by deeds, not fine words, and advised Lucilius to turn good thoughts into practice. The Stoic advice to someone inspired is simple: let the impulse become action, even a small one — and don't make it a condition that inspiration last forever. Work begun on the upswing can be calmly continued when the upswing subsides.
inspiration.practice: Take the first step while the surge is still warm: one line of a sketch, one call, one new file with a name. Seneca would say: a thought is tested by action.

quote.text: Philosophy teaches us to act, not to speak.
quote.author: Seneca

schadenfreude.text: Hands, feet and eyelids of one body, the upper and lower rows of teeth — this is how Marcus Aurelius saw people: to act against one another is against nature (II, 1). When someone else's failure brings a secret pleasure, people rarely admit it, but it doesn't make you a bad person. The Stoics would explain schadenfreude through the “impression”: somewhere inside, you assented to the thought that someone else's failure adds something to you — justice, room, relief from rivalry. Epictetus would object: a person's good lies in their own choice, their prohairesis, so another's failure adds nothing to your good and takes nothing away. Then schadenfreude is a signal: somewhere you feel shortchanged or hurt. That is exactly the place worth looking at — gently, without self-reproach.
schadenfreude.practice: When you notice schadenfreude, silently wish that person one simple good thing — a good night's sleep, a way through, a fix. Marcus would say: this is a hand helping a hand.

contempt.text: “Someone bathes hastily — don't say ‘badly,’ say ‘hastily,’” Epictetus taught (Enchiridion, 45). Contempt makes a person smaller in your eyes, and often fatigue, hurt or a wish to protect yourself lies behind that coldness. The Stoics themselves advised “despising” many things — fame, luxury, the opinion of the crowd — that is, seeing that these don't make a person better. But toward people themselves, Marcus Aurelius took a different attitude: someone who errs does so out of ignorance of what is good and what is bad, and yet remains your kin in reason. How do you know why a person does what they do, Epictetus asked. The Stoics would say that contempt is a judgment, not a fact. You can notice it and split it in two: what the person actually did — and what verdict I added to it.
contempt.practice: Retell to yourself the act that stirs your contempt using only facts and verbs, the way Epictetus would: “hastily,” not “badly.” Notice whether the feeling changes.

disgust.text: Marcus Aurelius once admired the cracks in a loaf's crust: they were no part of the baker's plan, yet somehow they please the eye (III, 2). In the same way, he wrote, to one who looks into nature even the foam at a lion's mouth and the wrinkles of old age have their own beauty. Disgust is an ancient bodily feeling that makes us recoil from what seems dirty, alien or spoiled; it can concern people, situations, and even ourselves. For a Stoic, disgust can be respected as a protection, but not taken as the last word: what provokes it is also part of nature, with its own order. And if disgust is turned on yourself, a Stoic would remind you: neither your body nor your mistakes exhaust who you are — what matters most in you is the capacity to judge and to choose.
disgust.practice: Look at what disgusts you, or at its image in your mind, with the eyes of Marcus the naturalist: shape, color, what it's made of, what role it plays in nature. Two minutes, no adjectives of judgment.

revenge.text: “Revenge is an inhuman word, though it passes for a just one,” Seneca observes (On Anger, II, 32). The wish to pay someone back is a natural response to pain inflicted on you: it carries a sense of justice and a need for your pain to be acknowledged. In On Anger, Seneca examined exactly this thirst for retribution and considered it the most destructive part of anger: revenge makes us serve the one who hurt us — think about them, spend our time and strength on them. A Stoic would say that the wish for revenge is at first only a “first movement,” and you are not responsible for its arising; but you decide whether to assent to the thought “I must pay them back.” You can acknowledge: I'm hurting, I was treated unfairly — and direct your strength toward protecting yourself and your boundaries rather than toward harming someone else. That way you remain the master of your own life, not an extension of someone else's act.
revenge.practice: Say out loud — to yourself or to someone close: “I'm hurting, I was treated unfairly, and what I need protection from is…” Finish with one calm step that harms no one.

quote.text: The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong doer.
quote.author: Marcus Aurelius

anger_at_loved.text: “Everything has two handles,” Epictetus said: by one it can be carried, by the other it cannot. When you love someone and suddenly find yourself boiling at them, and afterward feel ashamed, that is very human: with those closest to us we are least defended. If your brother wrongs you, don't take hold of the handle “he has wronged me” — it cannot be carried that way; take hold of the other: “he is my brother, we were brought up together” (Enchiridion, 43). This doesn't cancel your anger — it may point to an important need. Every evening Seneca reviewed the day that had passed, calmly and without self-flagellation: where did I flare up, what touched a nerve, how will I act differently? The Stoics would say that an outburst doesn't cancel love; it shows the spot where a pause is needed next time.
anger_at_loved.practice: Pick up a cup by its handle and say to yourself the other “handle” of the situation: “He is my brother” — or “she is my mom, we've been through a lot.” Hold it like that for a minute.

ambivalence.text: The Stoic Hierocles pictured life as a set of circles: at the center, myself; then family, relatives, fellow citizens, all of humanity — and the task is to draw the circles closer to the center. But what do you do when the closest circle warms and irritates at once, when you love someone and can't stand them? This tangled state happens far more often than people usually admit. The Stoics would help untangle this knot. For them, a person close to you is not wholly “good” or wholly “bad,” but a living human being, with actions in their own power and traits you don't get to choose. For the Stoics, the bond with those close to us is not only a feeling but a chosen attitude. You don't have to demand of yourself a whole, uniform love: it is enough to distinguish what exactly stirs tenderness and what stirs irritation, and to respond to each separately.
ambivalence.practice: Imagine this person in Hierocles' circle next to you. Name one trait that makes you want to draw them closer, and one that calls for distance — and let both be true.

guilty_relief.text: Seneca confesses to Lucilius that he once mourned his friend Annaeus Serenus so hard that grief overpowered him — and advises something else: in time, to remember those who are gone with joy (Letter LXIII). Relief after losing someone close, especially after a long illness, is a feeling many people secretly blame themselves for. But relief and love can live side by side. A long heaviness — caregiving, fear, powerlessness — wears a person down, and when it ends, body and mind naturally breathe out. For a Stoic, this is a “first movement,” not a verdict on your love. Seneca did not demand uniform sorrow. Epictetus would remind you: you are answerable for how you acted, not for which feeling rose up on its own. Relief speaks of how hard it was — not of your having loved less.
guilty_relief.practice: Say quietly, out loud: “I feel lighter because it was very hard.” Say it once more, more slowly, and notice that the love hasn't gone anywhere because of these words.

indifference.text: Epictetus compared life to a play: the author chooses the role, and our business is to play the one we were given well (Enchiridion, 17). Sometimes something ought to move you — someone's misfortune, important news — and yet inside it's quiet, and that is frightening: “Is something wrong with me?” The Stoics are often pictured as preachers of unfeelingness, but that isn't accurate: their apatheia is not indifference but freedom from overwhelming passions, alongside a living care for others. The Stoics would probably note that a lull sometimes comes after long overstrain, like silence after noise, and in itself says nothing about your kindness. What the Stoics considered most important was not the strength of a feeling but intention and action: in On Benefits, Seneca wrote that the value of a good deed lies in the will of the one who does it. You can care even when emotion is silent. The feeling may come back later, and for now action is enough.
indifference.practice: Play your role in one small scene: make a call, help carry something, answer a message — without demanding that you feel anything. Then simply note: done.

escape.text: “Why be surprised, when you take yourself along wherever you go?” — so, according to Seneca, Socrates answered a man whom travel did not help (Letter XXVIII). The wish to drop everything and leave — change your job, your city, your role — is strongest when the load has long been more than you can bear, and Seneca treated it with sympathy. The point is not that you mustn't leave, but that part of the weight travels with us. Seneca suggested sorting it out: what exactly am I running from — the place, or the way I live in it? Epictetus would add: look at what here is in your power. Sometimes a change is a sensible choice; sometimes it is enough to change the inner order of things. The urge to get away is an honest signal that something needs to change.
escape.practice: Take a short walk, like a small escape, and ask yourself on the way: what exactly am I running from — the place, or the way I live in it? What of it came along on the walk with me?

forbidden_attraction.text: Epictetus advised saying to a vivid impression: “Wait, let me see who you are and what you're about” (Discourses, II, 18) — and among his examples is precisely a person's beauty. Attraction to someone who is unavailable or “not the right one” is unsettling: it arises on its own, without asking permission. The Stoics help lift some of the guilt from it. Attraction itself is a “first movement,” an impression that comes without our consent; Epictetus taught that which “impressions” come to us is not in our power, but how we deal with them is. You can ask: what exactly draws me — the person themselves, or what they represent for me: freedom, attention, a different life? Such a question passes no verdicts and commands nothing; it simply gives you back clarity and the right to decide for yourself.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Say silently to this impression, as Epictetus advised: “Wait, let me take a look.” Then name in one word what it promises: freedom, attention, a different life?

social_anxiety.text: Each of us loves ourselves more than anyone, yet values others' opinion of us above our own, Marcus Aurelius marveled (XII, 4). When people look at you and it feels as if you are being weighed, shyness and fear of judgment come over a great many of us. Epictetus, a former slave, thought a great deal about other people's opinions and considered them the prime example of what is “not in our power”: what others think of you is up to them. It sounds like bad news, but there is freedom in it — you can stop being responsible for what goes on in other people's heads. He even advised: if you want to make progress, be content to be thought ignorant in external matters (Enchiridion, 13). A Stoic would say that your task in a conversation is to be honest and kind; the impression you make is no longer your job.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, put a hand on your chest and choose one intention within your power — for example, “to listen attentively.” Afterward, judge yourself only by that, not by how you came across.

uncertainty.text: The Stoics advised adding a few words to any plan — “if nothing prevents it”: I will sail to Rome, if nothing prevents it. Not knowing is exhausting: the mind wants to know how everything will end, and there is no answer. The Stoics lived in a world where war, exile or illness could come at any moment — and they developed a particular attitude toward this. This “reserve clause” means: intend, do everything you can, and accept that the outcome is not in your hands. Such action doesn't depend on the outcome: your part is done even if the result turns out differently. Marcus Aurelius suggested not troubling yourself by picturing your whole life at once, but asking what in the present moment is truly unbearable (VIII, 36). The Stoics would say that uncertainty is not a malfunction but the ordinary state of the world; your support comes not from knowing the future, but from clarity about how you will respond to whatever comes.
uncertainty.practice: Say one plan for tomorrow out loud the Stoic way, with the reserve clause: “I'll do this — if nothing prevents it.” Notice how the feeling in your chest changes.

waiting.text: “The greatest obstacle to living is expectancy, which depends on tomorrow and loses today,” Seneca wrote in On the Shortness of Life. Waiting for results, an answer or news can be more agonizing than the answer itself: life seems to be put on pause. The Stoics didn't suggest you stop waiting — that's impossible — but they suggested a distinction: the outcome is in other hands, but how you live today is up to you. Epictetus would say: the letter will come or not regardless of how many times you check your phone; but this evening, a conversation with a friend, a walk — those are yours. For a Stoic, waiting can be accepted as a background, without handing it all your time. Waiting and living at the same time is a skill too, and one you can learn.
waiting.practice: Put your phone in a drawer for half an hour and take up one task that doesn't depend on the answer — water the plants, cook something, go for a walk. The answer will come or not without your checking.

quote.text: The greatest obstacle to living is expectancy, which hangs upon tomorrow and loses today.
quote.author: Seneca

regret.text: “I made a prosperous voyage when I was shipwrecked,” Zeno used to say: it was the loss of his cargo that brought the merchant from Citium to Athens, and to philosophy. Regret over what you did or didn't do is a sign that you care how you live. The Stoics looked at the past soberly: it is no longer in our power, and it can't be changed. Marcus Aurelius reminded himself that each of us lives only in the present instant, and the rest is either already lived or unknown (III, 10). But this is not a call to forget. Seneca reviewed each day every evening and admitted that he did so without fear, since he could say to himself: “See that you don't do that again; this time I pardon you” (On Anger, III, 36). A Stoic would say that regret is useful when it becomes a lesson, and tormenting when it becomes a verdict. The past can be turned into understanding, and understanding into your next action.
regret.practice: Say to yourself one sentence in Zeno's spirit about your own “shipwreck”: “This mistake taught me…” End with Seneca's words: “This time I pardon you.”

longing.text: Seneca confessed to Lucilius that when a letter from him arrived, it was as if he saw his friend beside him: it holds real traces, a hand one recognizes (Letter XL). When you miss one particular person, general words hardly console, and the Stoics did not consider this feeling a weakness. Seneca believed that closeness can be kept in our thoughts: a friend we think of is, in a sense, with us. At the same time, the Stoics reminded us that the people we love are not in our power and are not given to us forever. The thought is bitter, but it teaches us to treasure every meeting and every letter. The Stoics would say that longing speaks of the value of a bond; you can allow it to be, and at the same time sustain that bond — with a word, a memory, something you would have done together.
longing.practice: Close your eyes and relive one shared minute with this person in every detail: the light, the voice, the smell, what was in your hands. Seneca would say: right now they are with you.

world_pain.text: Part of the Meditations was written in an army camp while plague was spreading through the empire — and many of Marcus Aurelius's pages are about how not to grow hardened. Heavy news, wars and injustice hurt a sensitive person, and that is a sign that you feel your connection with others. The Stoics called the human being a “cosmopolitan,” a citizen of the world: we belong not only to our own city but to all of humanity. The Stoic response to pain for the world has two parts. The first is to distinguish what is in your power: not the outcome of world events, but your kindness, help for those nearby, honesty. The second is not to confuse compassion with endless immersion in the news: that drains you, and the world needs people who still have strength left. You can carry this pain without letting it break you.
world_pain.practice: Do one good deed within your reach — help a neighbor, support someone nearby, make a call. Then, like Marcus after a day in camp, give yourself an hour without news.

rejection.text: Diogenes, from whom the Stoics learned not to depend on others' opinion, begged alms from a statue — “to get used to being refused.” A refusal, coldness, a closed door feel like a judgment of your whole self, and that hurts. Epictetus would say that two things are mixed together here: another person's decision, which is not in your power, and your worth, which doesn't depend on it. The Enchiridion (25) has a parable: you weren't invited to the banquet — which means you didn't pay the price it is sold for, flattery and fawning, and you kept what you didn't give away. For a Stoic, someone else's “no” is a fact about their choice, not a verdict on you. That doesn't cancel the pain: the first movements of hurt and sadness are natural. But you don't have to assent to the added judgment “so I'm worth nothing.” Rejection shows how much you wanted connection — and this capacity to reach toward people stays with you.
rejection.practice: If you like, try Diogenes' small exercise: ask today for something trivial where a refusal costs nothing — a different table, directions from a passerby. Notice: the “no” was said, and you are still whole.

abandonment.text: Seneca wrote that the wise person is content with himself — and yet still wishes to have a friend, a neighbor, a companion (Letter IX). When you are afraid of being left, it seems that without this person your foothold will vanish. The Stoics wouldn't brush this feeling aside, but they would suggest looking gently at where your foothold actually is. Epictetus taught that those close to us are the most precious thing, but not “ours” in the sense of being fully in our power: their decisions belong to them. From this he drew a conclusion that is not cold but freeing: you can love without clutching, and look for support within yourself too — in your capacity to choose, to care, to build connections. A Stoic would say that the fear of losing a bond speaks of its value; at the same time, you can strengthen what doesn't depend on a single person.
abandonment.practice: Draw Hierocles' circles around yourself in your mind, and in each find one person, place or activity that holds you up. Simply notice that they are there.

unrequited.text: “If you would be loved, love” — Seneca quotes this recipe of the Stoic Hecato and promises it works better than any love potion (Letter IX). When the feeling is there but there is no answer, it is one of the oldest human pains. The Stoics wouldn't say you love “in vain.” Love, as they understood it, can be an expression of goodwill, of wishing the other well — and that is a worthy feeling. But they would point to an important distinction: your feeling is yours, you can accept it and give it direction, while the other person's feeling is not in your power. Epictetus considered attempts to control what is beyond our power the chief source of torment. Hecato's recipe is not a promise of reciprocity but a reminder that the capacity to love remains yours. You can respect your love without demanding an answer from it.
unrequited.practice: Do one kind thing today for someone else — not for this person. Notice: the capacity to love works even without an answer.

humiliation.text: When someone spat in Cato's face, he wiped it off and said: “Now I can assure everyone that they are wrong who say you have no mouth” (Seneca, On Anger, III, 38). Humiliation burns: it seems your dignity has been taken in front of everyone. The Stoics thought about this a great deal, for among them were both the slave Epictetus and the senator Seneca, who lived through exile. Their central idea: dignity is not something that can be taken from outside. The person who humiliated you has command over their own words and actions, but not over whether you agree with their assessment. This doesn't mean they are right or that there is no pain. It means that the last word about your worth remains yours. In On the Constancy of the Wise Man, Seneca wrote that an insult can wound a person, but cannot diminish one whose support lies within. The Stoics would say that humiliation says more about the act of the one who humiliated than about you.
humiliation.practice: Straighten your back, feel your feet on the ground, and say under your breath: “Whatever this person did, my dignity lies in my own actions.” Name one of your actions that you respect.

quote.text: Remember that it is not he who reviles you or strikes you who insults you, but it is your opinion about these things as being insulting.
quote.author: Epictetus

body_shame.text: Seneca describes his friend Claranus: a frail, plain body, and a soul such that it seems to have chosen a modest dwelling on purpose (Letter LXVI). Being unhappy with your body is a common and often quiet pain. The Stoics counted the body among the “indifferents” — that's their term: not something trivial, but something that makes a person neither good nor bad. Among the indifferents there are “preferred” ones — health, strength — but your worth doesn't live there. A great and beautiful soul, Seneca wrote, can live in any body and is not diminished by it in the least. For a Stoic, the body is not a shop window for other people's eyes but a companion you can be grateful to for what it does. Standards of beauty change from age to age, but the capacity to be kind and honest stays yours in any body.
body_shame.practice: Run your palm along your arm from shoulder to wrist and name three things your body did for you today: carried you, kept you warm, let you taste something. Thank it, the way Marcus thanked his teachers.

illness.text: Epictetus, who was lame, said: “Illness is an impediment to the body, but not to choice”; lameness hinders the leg, but not you (Enchiridion, 9). When your body lets you down, it is frightening and exhausting: plans collapse, and your strength goes into simply getting through the day. The Stoics didn't regard illness as a cause for shame and didn't demand a show of cheerfulness. Seneca was ill a great deal throughout his life and wrote honestly to Lucilius about his ailments. In one letter (LXXVIII) he tells how in illness he was helped by his friends, their care and their conversation, and that a sick person still has important work of their own: not letting fear inflate the suffering, and finding what still brings joy. A Stoic would say that illness is neither your fault nor your essence. Your task is not to “defeat” it by willpower, but to find what remains in your power today: attention, a thought, a kind word.
illness.practice: Let someone take care of you — accept help, or simply talk with a friend, as Seneca did when ill. Let everything else not be your job today.

quote.text: Disease is an impediment to the body, but not to the will, unless the will itself chooses.
quote.author: Epictetus

pride.text: A vine that has borne its grapes seeks no witnesses and no rewards — this is how Marcus Aurelius described a person who has done a good deed (V, 6). Pride in what you've done is a good feeling, and there's no need to hide it. The Stoics distinguished vanity, which lives on other people's praise, from the eupatheiai — good, rational feelings, among which is calm joy. The joy of a job well done belongs precisely to this realm: it rests not on others' opinion but on your own action. The Stoics would say that healthy pride can be recognized by the fact that it needs no comparison with others and does not fear their indifference. Let yourself feel it: you put your strength and your choice into this.
pride.practice: Sit for a minute like a vine after harvest: adding nothing, showing it to no one. Name to yourself which of your qualities went into it — persistence, honesty, care.

melancholy.text: “Leaves — some the wind scatters on the ground, others the forest brings forth in spring; so is the generation of men” — Marcus Aurelius copies out these lines of Homer for himself (X, 34). In bright sadness, sorrow mingles with tenderness toward the world, and the Stoics, strangely enough, knew it well. Marcus Aurelius kept returning to the thought that everything flows. In his hands this sounds not like despair but like an ability to see the beauty of what passes. Seneca wrote that fruit is most welcome when its season is almost over (Letter XII) — and that later years have their own charm. For a Stoic, melancholy can be a kind of clear sight: you see that nothing is eternal, and so your attention to life becomes more tender. There's no need to chase it away; you can give it a little time.
melancholy.practice: Step outside for a few minutes or open a window and find something that will soon change: the light, the leaves, the clouds. Look at it the way Marcus looked at leaves — unhurried, drawing no conclusions.
